questions.q: Your teacher asks you to time a quiz with a bottle water clock. Describe three steps you would follow to make it and use it.
questions.a: Make a hole in the cap, place the upper half inverted over the lower and fill it; mark the level every minute with a watch; pour the water back and count the marks it touches.
s: Makes a small hole in the cap and fills the inverted upper part with water
Marks the water level after every minute using a watch
Reads time by pouring the water back and counting marks touched

questions.q: Zoya says, "A sundial always gives the same time as a wristwatch set to Indian Standard Time, anywhere in India." Check her claim.
questions.a: Not correct. A sundial measures local or solar time, so a correction is needed to find Indian Standard Time.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
Reason: a sundial measures local (solar) time from the Sun's shadow
Says a correction is needed to get Indian Standard Time

questions.q: Two identical bottle water clocks hold the same amount of water, but the cap of clock B has a bigger hole than clock A. Rohan wants to use the minute marks made for clock A on clock B. What will happen?
questions.a: A bigger hole changes how fast the water drips, so the minute marks of clock A are wrong for clock B; marks must be made again against a watch.
o: B empties sooner, so it needs new marks made with a watch
Both clocks empty together because the water quantity is the same
B shows time better because the water drips out faster
B takes longer to empty because a bigger hole is harder to fill

questions.q: Neeta makes the bottle water clock of Activity 8.1 and numbers the minute marks 1, 2, 3 ... from the top as the level falls. (a) How often does she mark the water level while it drips? (b) Later the level touches the 9th mark. How much time has passed?
questions.a: (a) After every 1 minute, using a watch. (b) 9 marks means 9 minutes.
s: Part (a): marks after every one minute using a watch
Part (b): 9 minutes from the number of marks

questions.q: Ritu builds the bottle water clock of Activity 8.1 and marks the water level every minute with a watch, numbering the marks 1, 2, 3 ... from the top as the level falls. Later she pours the lower water back and the level in the upper half touches the 6th mark. What does this show?
questions.a: Each mark stands for one minute, so touching the 6th mark means 6 minutes have passed.
o: 6 minutes have passed since she poured it back
6 litres of water have dripped into the lower half
The water has been dripping for 6 hours so far
The hole has become 6 times smaller than before

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A floating bowl with a fine hole in a water clock measures the same interval each time it sinks.
Reason (R): An hourglass measures time by the flow of sand from one bulb to another.
questions.a: Both true. R describes a different device and does not explain why the bowl gives a fixed interval (the hole sets a fixed filling time).
o: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q: Create a short situation in which a person needs a timer that works without sunlight and without electricity. Name the early device you would give her and justify the choice.
questions.a: Example: A student must time 10 minutes of silent reading in the evening during a power cut. A candle clock or hourglass works because it needs no sunlight and no electricity.
s: Gives a realistic situation without sunlight or electricity
Names a suitable device such as a candle clock, hourglass or water clock
Justifies: it does not depend on a shadow or on electricity

questions.q: Name two devices, other than a sundial and a water clock, that people made to measure short intervals within a day, and state what each uses.
questions.a: Hourglass: sand flows from one bulb to the other. Candle clock: a marked candle shows how much time has passed as it burns.
s: Hourglass uses flow of sand from one bulb to another
Candle clock uses markings on a burning candle

questions.q: In the earliest form of timekeeping described in the chapter, a day was defined by which repeating event?
questions.a: A day was defined by the cycle of rising and setting of the Sun. Moon phases and seasons are longer cycles also used for timekeeping.
o: The rising and setting of the Sun
The changing phases of the Moon
The changing of the seasons
The swing of a lamp hung from a ceiling

questions.q: A school camp needs a timer in four situations. Choose the most suitable early device for each and justify the choice: (i) timing a short interval in a dark room, (ii) noticing the hours pass in a sunny courtyard, (iii) timing a long evening programme against equal markings, (iv) a device that is lifted and restarted again and again after a fixed interval. Then say which of your four fails after sunset.
questions.a: Hourglass for the dark room (sand flow); sundial for the sunny courtyard (shadow); candle clock for the evening programme (markings burn); floating-bowl water clock for repeated fixed intervals. The sundial fails after sunset as no shadow forms.
s: Dark room: hourglass, since sand flows without sunlight
Sunny courtyard: sundial, since the shadow position shows time
Evening programme: candle clock with markings
Restarted again and again: floating bowl water clock that fills and sinks in a fixed time
Sundial fails after sunset because there is no sunlight to cast a shadow

questions.q: After a floating-bowl water clock sinks, it is lifted up and floated again. Why is this done?
questions.a: The bowl fills and sinks in a fixed time; refloating it starts the next equal interval.
o: So that the same fixed interval can be measured once more
So that the hole becomes larger and the bowl fills faster
So that sand can run back into the upper bulb
So that the shadow can fall on the scale again

questions.q: "Timekeeping began with nature and then moved to devices." Justify this statement using the Sun's cycle, calendars and at least two devices.
questions.a: People noticed repeating events such as sunrise and sunset, Moon phases and seasons and made calendars, with a day defined by sunrise and sunset. To measure smaller intervals they made devices such as the sundial (shadow) and the hourglass (sand). Each device relies on something that repeats or flows steadily.
s: Natural events repeat after definite intervals (Sun, Moon, seasons)
Calendars first; a day defined by sunrise and sunset
Needed smaller intervals within a day
Names two devices with how each works
Concludes that devices copied a steady repeating process

questions.q:
Match Column I with Column II.
1. Sundial
2. Floating bowl with a fine hole
3. Hourglass
4. Candle clock
a. Burns down against markings
b. Flow of sand between bulbs
c. Shadow of an object
d. Fills and sinks in a fixed time
questions.a: Sundial - shadow (c); floating bowl - fills and sinks in fixed time (d); hourglass - sand (b); candle clock - burning markings (a).

questions.q:
Statement I: A sundial shows time from the changing position of a shadow.
Statement II: A floating bowl with a fine hole fills and sinks after a fixed time.
Statement III: An hourglass measures time by the burning of a marked candle.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: I and II are correct. III is false: the hourglass uses sand flowing between bulbs; burning markings belong to the candle clock.
o: I and II only
II and III only
I and III only
I, II and III

questions.q: (a) Name the device that shows time from the shadow of an object. (b) Give one reason it cannot be used to tell time at night.
questions.a: (a) Sundial. (b) At night there is no sunlight to cast a shadow, so there is no shadow position to read.
s: Part (a): names the sundial
Part (b): says it needs sunlight to cast a shadow

questions.q:
Shalini visits her grandparents in a village in Rajasthan. In the courtyard a pointed stone stands on a flat slab, and the villagers once used the moving shadow of its tip to decide the time for collecting milk. Milk must be collected at 7:00 am every day, also through the monsoon. On a rainy day last week no shadow could be seen and the milk collector came late. Shalini's cousin suggests a candle clock: a 12 cm candle marked so that 1 cm burns in 10 minutes.
(a) Name this device and say what changes through the day to show time.
(b) Why could nobody read the time on the rainy day?
(c) For how long will the 12 cm candle show time once lit?
(d) Decide how the family should arrange milk collection on clear and on rainy mornings, and say what must be done each day for the candle clock to help.
questions.a: (a) Sundial; shadow position. (b) No sunlight, so no shadow. (c) 120 minutes = 2 hours. (d) Read the sundial on clear mornings; on rainy mornings light the candle at a known time, 5:00 am, because a candle clock shows only the time since it was lit and 2 h of burning ends at 7:00 am.
s: Part (a): sundial; the position of the shadow changes
Part (b): no clear shadow forms without sunlight
Part (c): 12 x 10 = 120 minutes, i.e. 2 hours
Part (d): sundial on clear mornings, candle clock on rainy ones, lit at a known time such as 5:00 am so that it burns out at 7:00 am

questions.q: Which statement about early time-measuring devices is false?
questions.a: The false statement is that a sundial works at any hour; it needs sunlight to cast a shadow, so it cannot work at night.
o: A sundial can measure time at any hour of the day or night
A candle clock has markings that show time as it burns
A floating bowl with a fine hole fills and sinks in a fixed time
An hourglass measures time by sand flowing between two bulbs

questions.q: What is meant by a repeating event in nature? Give two examples that humans used for timekeeping.
questions.a: An event that happens again after a definite interval of time, such as the rising and setting of the Sun, the phases of the Moon or the changing seasons.
s: States that it repeats after a definite interval
Gives two examples such as sunrise and sunset, Moon phases, seasons

questions.q: In a sundial, which thing changes through the day so that time can be read?
questions.a: A sundial shows time from the changing position of the shadow of an object cast by sunlight.
o: The position of the shadow of the pointer
The level of water in a bowl or vessel
The length of the marked candle as it burns
The amount of sand left in the upper bulb

questions.q: Differentiate between the two types of water clocks described in the chapter.
questions.a: In one type water flows out of a marked vessel; in the other a bowl with a fine hole floats on water, fills in a fixed time and sinks.
s: Outflow type: water flows out of a vessel with time markings
Floating-bowl type: bowl with a fine hole fills and sinks in a fixed time

questions.q:
Ishaan's group builds a bottle water clock for the school science fair, as in Activity 8.1. They fill the upper half with coloured water and mark the level after every one minute, numbering the marks 1, 2, 3 ... from the top as the level falls. All the water takes 9 minutes to drip down, so the marks run from 1 to 9. During a relay race at the fair, an observer sees the level touch the 5th mark when the race starts and the 8th mark when it ends. Later the teacher wants to time a 20-minute written test using this clock.
(a) Which instrument did the group need to make the marks, and why?
(b) How long did the relay race last?
(c) A second race lasts 4 minutes 30 seconds. Can this clock show that time exactly? Explain.
(d) Decide how the 9-minute clock can be used to time the 20-minute test.
questions.a: (a) A watch, so the marks stand for exact minutes. (b) 3 min. (c) No; only whole-minute marks exist, so 4 min 30 s lies halfway between two marks. (d) Run it twice for 18 min and then to the 2nd mark: 9 + 9 + 2 = 20 min.
s: Part (a): a watch, to know when each minute has passed
Part (b): 8 - 5 = 3 minutes
Part (c): no; marks are made only for whole minutes, so 4 min 30 s falls between the 4th and 5th marks
Part (d): use it twice (18 minutes) and a third time up to the 2-minute mark, 9 + 9 + 2 = 20

questions.q:
In an old town a temple uses a Ghatika-yantra, a bowl with a fine hole that fills and sinks in 24 minutes. The attendant starts it at sunrise, 6:00 am, lifts and refloats it after each sinking and strikes a gong each time. The town council wants every ghati announced, through the night as well, and can pay for only one arrangement: the bowl with an attendant, or a stone sundial that needs no attendant.
(a) At what time is the 5th gong struck?
(b) How many gongs will have been struck by 12:00 noon?
(c) The attendant dozes off for 72 minutes after one sinking without refloating the bowl. How many gongs are missed?
(d) Which arrangement should the council choose and why?
questions.a: (a) 8:00 am. (b) 15 gongs. (c) 3 gongs. (d) The bowl with an attendant, because a sundial cannot work at night, while the bowl gives equal 24-minute intervals day and night.
s: Part (a): 5 x 24 = 120 min, so 8:00 am
Part (b): 6 h = 360 min; 360 / 24 = 15 gongs
Part (c): 72 / 24 = 3 gongs missed
Part (d): the bowl; it works at night and gives a fixed 24-minute interval, whereas a sundial needs sunlight

questions.q: Why was the Ghatika-yantra a better design than the outflow water clock, and why was it only progressively replaced by pendulum clocks in the late nineteenth century? Answer in five steps: (i) the flaw of the outflow clock, (ii) how the bowl fixes it, (iii) the unit it gave, (iv) what finally replaced it, (v) where it still lived on.
questions.a: Outflow clocks slowed as the level dropped; the bowl fills and sinks in a fixed 24 minutes, giving the ghatika (60 a day). Pendulum clocks progressively replaced it in the late nineteenth century, but it continued at religious places for rituals.
s: Outflow flaw: flow rate decreased as the level dropped
Bowl with a fine hole fills and sinks in a fixed time
The fixed 24 minutes gave the ghatika, 60 to a day
Progressively replaced by pendulum clocks in the late nineteenth century
Continued at religious places for rituals

questions.q: (a) How long did the bowl of the Ghatika-yantra take to fill and sink? (b) Using this, show that a 24-hour day has 60 ghatis.
questions.a: (a) 24 minutes. (b) A day has 24 x 60 = 1440 minutes and 1440 / 24 = 60 ghatis.
s: Part (a): 24 minutes
Part (b): 24 x 60 = 1440 min in a day; 1440 / 24 = 60 ghatis

questions.q: The shadow on the scale of the Samrat Yantra moves at about 1 millimetre per second. (a) How far does it move in 2 seconds? (b) In 1 minute, in centimetres? (c) In 10 minutes, in centimetres? (d) Using (a), say why a finely marked scale can show intervals as short as 2 seconds. (e) Why must a reading be corrected to give IST?
questions.a: (a) 2 mm. (b) 60 mm = 6 cm. (c) 600 mm = 60 cm. (d) The shadow moves 2 mm in 2 s, which a fine scale can mark. (e) A sundial shows local solar time.
s: Part (a): 2 mm
Part (b): 60 mm = 6 cm
Part (c): 600 mm = 60 cm
Part (d): the shadow moves 2 mm, a distance that can be marked on a fine scale
Part (e): it shows local solar time, so a correction gives IST

questions.q: A 24-hour day was divided into how many equal ghatis?
questions.a: A day was divided into 60 equal ghatis. 24 is the hours and 1440 the minutes in a day.

questions.q: Anil reads the Samrat Yantra's shadow time at Jantar Mantar and finds it different from the Indian Standard Time on his phone. Which statement explains this?
questions.a: The chapter says that like any sundial it measures local or solar time, requiring a correction to find Indian Standard Time.
o: A sundial shows local solar time; a correction gives IST
The shadow of a very tall sundial moves faster than real time
The stone expands in afternoon heat and reads ahead of time
The scale is marked only in whole hours, not in seconds

questions.q: Which property of a pendulum, found by Galileo, made it useful for building a clock?
questions.a: Galileo found that the time for one oscillation is always the same for a pendulum of a given length, so it can mark equal intervals.
o: Each oscillation takes the same time for a given length
Its time period grows steadily with the mass of the bob
Its swings take longer and longer as time passes
It keeps swinging without needing any rigid support

questions.q: Rahul says, "Water clocks were given up as soon as mechanical clocks appeared in the fourteenth century." Check this using the chapter.
questions.a: Wrong. The Ghatika-yantra was progressively replaced by pendulum clocks only in the late nineteenth century and was still used at religious places.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
Ghatika-yantra was replaced progressively by pendulum clocks in the late nineteenth century
It continued to be used at religious places for rituals

questions.q: A priest starts a Ghatika-yantra at 5:00 am for a long ritual and refloats the bowl after each sinking, 25 times in all. How many minutes and hours does this take, and at what time does the 25th sinking happen?
questions.a: 25 sinkings x 24 min = 600 min = 10 h; the 25th sinking is at 3:00 pm.
s: 25 x 24 = 600 minutes
600 minutes = 10 hours

questions.q: A student says a Ghatika-yantra could announce 70 ghatis in one 24-hour day. Show with numbers that this is impossible.
questions.a: A day holds 1440 / 24 = 60 ghatis. 70 ghatis would need 70 x 24 = 1680 min = 28 h, more than a day.
s: Day = 24 x 60 = 1440 minutes so 1440 / 24 = 60 ghatis
70 x 24 = 1680 minutes
1680 minutes is 28 hours, more than the 24-hour day

questions.q:
Students from a Jaipur school visit the Samrat Yantra. The guide says it is about 300 years old, 27 metres high, and that its shadow moves at about 1 millimetre per second on a finely marked scale. A student notes that during the guide's talk the shadow edge moved 12 centimetres. Another student compares the reading with her phone, which shows Indian Standard Time, and sees a difference. The principal proposes that on sunny days a sundial like this should ring the 8:00 am assembly bell, with the wall clock used on cloudy days.
(a) How long was the guide's talk?
(b) How far will the shadow move in 15 minutes?
(c) Why does the reading differ from the phone?
(d) Do you support the principal's plan? Say what must be done to the sundial reading and what happens on a cloudy morning.
questions.a: (a) 120 s = 2 min. (b) 900 mm = 90 cm. (c) Local solar time differs from IST. (d) Support it with conditions: apply the correction to get IST, and keep the wall clock for cloudy mornings when there is no shadow.
s: Part (a): 12 cm = 120 mm, at 1 mm per second = 120 s = 2 minutes
Part (c): a sundial shows local solar time, not IST
Part (d): supports only with a correction applied to get IST; on a cloudy morning no shadow forms, so the wall clock is needed

questions.q: Name the two ways in which time was measured in ancient India, according to the chapter, and name the text of Kautilya that mentions shadows.
questions.a: By shadows and by water clocks; the Arthasastra of Kautilya has the earliest reference to shadow-based timekeeping.
s: Shadows and water clocks
Arthasastra

questions.q: Differentiate between the time shown by the Samrat Yantra and Indian Standard Time.
questions.a: A sundial such as the Samrat Yantra measures local (solar) time; Indian Standard Time is obtained after applying a correction.
s: Samrat Yantra shows local solar time
A correction is needed to get Indian Standard Time

questions.q:
Statement I: Water clocks with water flowing out were inaccurate because the flow rate decreased as the water level dropped.
Statement II: The Ghatika-yantra was first mentioned by Varahamihira.
Statement III: The pendulum clock came after the mechanical clocks driven by weights, gears and springs.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: I and III are correct. II is false: the Ghatika-yantra was first mentioned by Aryabhata; Varahamihira gave the accurate shadow expression.
o: I and III only
I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III

questions.q:
Match Column I with Column II.
1. Arthasastra
2. Varahamihira
3. Aryabhata
4. Christiaan Huygens
a. First mentioned the Ghatika-yantra
b. Invented the pendulum clock in 1656
c. Earliest reference to shadow-based timekeeping
d. Accurate shadow expression around 530 CE
questions.a: Arthasastra - earliest shadow reference (c); Varahamihira - accurate expression about 530 CE (d); Aryabhata - Ghatika-yantra (a); Huygens - pendulum clock (b).

questions.q: Which statement about the Samrat Yantra at Jantar Mantar, Jaipur is false?
questions.a: The false statement is that it needs no correction; like any sundial it shows local solar time and needs a correction to give Indian Standard Time.
o: It gives Indian Standard Time with no correction
It is the world's largest sundial made of stone
Its shadow moves at about 1 millimetre every second
It stands about 27 metres high at Jantar Mantar

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The sinking-bowl clock (Ghatika-yantra) was developed after the outflow water clock.
Reason (R): In outflow water clocks the flow rate decreased as the water level dropped, making them inaccurate.
questions.a: Both true and R explains A: the inaccuracy of outflow clocks led to the sinking-bowl design.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q: How was the sinking of the bowl announced in ancient times, and at which places was the Ghatika-yantra used?
questions.a: By drums, conch shells or a gong; at Buddhist monasteries, royal palaces and town squares.
s: Announced by drums, conch shells or striking a gong
Used at Buddhist monasteries, royal palaces, town squares

questions.q: In an old temple, an attendant refloats the Ghatika-yantra bowl each time it sinks and strikes a gong. Starting at sunrise he has struck the gong 5 times. How much time has passed since sunrise?
questions.a: Each sinking takes 24 minutes (one ghatika), and 5 x 24 = 120 min = 2 h. 1 h 40 min uses 20 min a sinking; 5 h treats a ghati as an hour.
o: 2 hours
1 hour 40 minutes
2 hours 24 minutes
5 hours

questions.q: Which text has the earliest reference to shadow-based time measurement mentioned in the chapter?
questions.a: The Arthasastra by Kautilya has the earliest reference. The Sardulakarnavadana is named for the outflow water clock.
o: The Arthasastra by Kautilya
The Sardulakarnavadana
The work of Aryabhata
The work of Varahamihira

questions.q: (a) Who invented the pendulum clock, and in which century? (b) Name two kinds of parts that drove the mechanical clocks made from the fourteenth century.
questions.a: (a) Christiaan Huygens, in 1656, which is the seventeenth century. (b) Weights, gears and springs.
s: Part (a): Christiaan Huygens, in the seventeenth century (1656)
Part (b): any two of weights, gears and springs

questions.q: A pendulum has a time period of 1.5 s. How long will it take to complete 8 oscillations?
questions.a: Time = 8 x 1.5 s = 12 s. 5.3 s comes from 8 / 1.5; 9.5 s from adding; 0.19 s from 1.5 / 8.

questions.q: At a school playground two swings have chains of the same length; treat each swing as a simple pendulum. Tara is heavier than Arjun. Each is timed for 10 swings, released gently. What is the most likely result?
questions.a: The time period depends on length and not on mass, so equal lengths give almost equal times.
o: The two times will be almost equal because the length is the same
Tara's swing will take more time as a heavier bob takes longer
Arjun's swing will take more time as a lighter bob falls slower
No comparison is possible unless both are pushed equally hard

questions.q:
Pooja must set up a lab pendulum that completes one oscillation every 2 seconds (30 oscillations in a minute). In the store room she finds a 100 cm thread, a 150 cm thread, a 50 g bob and a 200 g bob. She times 10 oscillations for three set-ups. Set-up 1: 100 cm thread, 50 g bob, 20.0 s. Set-up 2: 150 cm thread, 50 g bob, 24.6 s. Set-up 3: 100 cm thread, 200 g bob, 20.1 s.
(a) Find the time period of each set-up.
(b) What do set-ups 1 and 3 show about the bob's mass?
(c) What do set-ups 1 and 2 show about the length?
(d) Which thread and bob should Pooja choose, and does her choice of bob matter?
questions.a: (a) 2.00 s, 2.46 s, 2.01 s. (b) Mass does not change the period. (c) The longer thread gives the longer period. (d) The 100 cm thread, with either bob.
s: Part (a): 2.00 s, 2.46 s and 2.01 s
Part (b): almost equal periods, so mass does not matter
Part (c): the longer thread has the longer time period
Part (d): the 100 cm thread, with either bob; the bob choice does not matter

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A pendulum of a given length can be used to measure time.
Reason (R): The time period of a simple pendulum of a given length is constant at a place.
questions.a: Both true and R explains A: a constant time period marks equal intervals, so the pendulum can measure time.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q: A pendulum completes 15 oscillations in 30 s. (a) Find its time period. (b) How many oscillations will it complete in 1 minute?
questions.a: (a) 2 s. (b) 60 s / 2 s = 30 oscillations.
s: Part (b): 60 / 2 = 30 oscillations

questions.q: Priya measures the time for 10 oscillations of her pendulum three times and gets 24.0 s, 23.8 s and 24.2 s. Her friend says the experiment has gone wrong because the readings are not identical. What is the best reply?
questions.a: The chapter says the time period is almost the same every time; tiny differences are not a fault.
o: They are almost equal, as a constant time period gives
She must repeat the trials until all three readings are exactly equal
The length of the thread must have changed between the three trials
The mass of the bob must have changed between the three trials

questions.q: Three students record the time for 10 oscillations. A: 64 cm thread, 100 g bob, 16.1 s. B: 64 cm thread, 250 g bob, 16.0 s. C: 121 cm thread, 100 g bob, 22.0 s. (a) Find each time period. (b) Compare A and B: does mass matter? (c) Compare A and C: what does length do? (d) A says, "B's reading is 0.1 s smaller, so heavier bobs swing faster." Is she right? (e) What would you change to make a pendulum's time period longer?
questions.a: (a) 1.61 s, 1.60 s, 2.20 s. (b) Almost equal, so mass does not matter. (c) Longer thread, longer period. (d) No; the 0.1 s is ordinary variation at the same length. (e) Lengthen the thread.
s: Part (a): 1.61 s, 1.60 s and 2.20 s
Part (b): the periods are almost equal, so mass does not matter
Part (c): the longer thread has the longer time period
Part (d): not right; the small difference is the usual variation, since length is the same
Part (e): lengthen the thread

questions.q: Name the two precautions the book asks you to take while releasing the bob in Activity 8.2.
questions.a: Take care not to push the bob while releasing it, and make sure the string is taut.
s: Do not push the bob while releasing it
Keep the string taut

questions.q: Define the time period of a pendulum and state its SI unit.
questions.a: The time taken by the pendulum to complete one oscillation; its SI unit is the second, s.
s: Time taken to complete one oscillation
SI unit is the second (s)

questions.q: Which path of the bob of a simple pendulum, from the mean position O with extremes A and B, is one complete oscillation?
questions.a: One oscillation is O to A to B and back to O (or A to B and back to A). O to A and back to O is only half of that.
o: O to A, then to B, then back to O
O to A and then straight back to O
O to B and stop at the extreme position
A to the mean position O and no further

questions.q: A student claims that the same pendulum took 20 s for 10 oscillations and also 40 s for 25 oscillations, both at the same place. Show that both readings cannot be true.
questions.a: 2 s versus 1.6 s. The time period of a pendulum of a given length is constant at a place, so the readings contradict each other.
s: Time period from first reading = 20 / 10 = 2 s
Time period from second reading = 40 / 25 = 1.6 s
A pendulum of given length has one constant time period, so 2 s and 1.6 s cannot both hold

questions.q: Dev says, "If I replace my iron ball with a lighter one on the same thread, the time period of my pendulum will stay the same." Do you agree?
questions.a: Yes. The time period depends on the length and not on the bob's mass, so with the same thread length at the same place it stays the same.
s: Verdict: agree
The time period depends on length, not on the bob's mass
It holds for the same length at the same place

questions.q:
At a mela a swing has chains of equal length. The operator times Ananya's ride and finds that she completes 12 oscillations in 30 seconds. Her younger brother Veer, who is lighter, then takes the same swing. The swing is available for 2 hours (120 minutes) and 40 children are waiting. Changing riders takes 30 seconds. The operator can offer either a ride of 3 minutes or a ride of 60 oscillations.
(a) Find the time period of Ananya's swing.
(b) How many oscillations are there in a 3-minute ride?
(c) What happens to the time period when lighter Veer rides? Why?
(d) Which ride option lets all 40 children ride, and why?
questions.a: (a) 2.5 s. (b) 72. (c) It stays almost the same; mass does not matter. (d) The 60-oscillation ride: 150 s + 30 s = 3 min per child, 120 min in all. The 3-minute ride needs 3.5 min per child, 140 min, which does not fit.
s: Part (b): 180 / 2.5 = 72 oscillations
Part (c): almost unchanged, since mass does not affect the time period
Part (d): 60 oscillations = 150 s, plus 30 s changing = 3 min a child, 40 x 3 = 120 min fits; the 3-minute ride needs 40 x 3.5 = 140 min

questions.q: On which one of the following does the time period of a simple pendulum depend, according to the chapter?
questions.a: The time period depends on the length but not on the bob's mass.
o: The length of the thread
The mass of the bob
The number of oscillations counted
The person who releases the bob

questions.q: Which item is NOT needed for the pendulum experiment of Activity 8.2?
questions.a: The activity uses a string, a heavy ball or stone as bob, a watch, a ruler and a rigid support, not a spring.
o: A spring
A stopwatch or watch
A ruler
A rigid support

questions.q: Design an experiment to show that the mass of the bob does not change the time period. Give five steps including how you would conclude.
questions.a: Fix the length at about 100 cm. Use bobs of different masses one by one. Time 10 oscillations for each and divide by 10. If the time periods are almost equal, mass does not affect the time period.
s: Keep the length of the thread the same
Use bobs of different mass
Time 10 oscillations for each bob
Divide by 10 to get each time period
Compare: nearly equal values mean mass does not matter

questions.q:
Statement I: One oscillation is complete when the bob goes from O to A and then straight back to O.
Statement II: The time period is the time for n oscillations divided by n.
Statement III: All pendulums of the same length have the same time period at a given place.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: II and III are correct. I is false: a full oscillation needs the bob to reach both extremes and return, O to A to B and back to O.
o: II and III only
I and II only
I and III only
I, II and III

questions.q: What is meant by saying that the motion of a pendulum is periodic?
questions.a: The bob repeats its path after a fixed interval of time.
s: It repeats its path
After a fixed interval of time

questions.q: In three trials of Activity 8.2 the time for 10 oscillations was 25.2 s, 24.8 s and 25.0 s. (a) Find the mean time for 10 oscillations. (b) Find the time period.
Describe in three steps how you would test whether the time period of a pendulum depends on its length.
questions.a: Take the same bob on threads of, say, 50 cm, 100 cm and 150 cm. Time 10 oscillations of each and divide by 10. Compare the time periods.
s: Uses three or more lengths with the same bob
Times 10 oscillations for each and divides by 10
Compares the time periods to see if they change

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Atomic clocks are more precise than Huygens' early pendulum clocks.
Reason (R): Atomic clocks work by the vibrations of a quartz crystal.
questions.a: A is true: atomic clocks lose one second in millions of years, early pendulum clocks gained or lost 10 s a day. R is false: atomic clocks use specific atoms; the quartz crystal belongs to quartz clocks.
o: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true

questions.q: An ECG machine records variations of a millisecond in heartbeats. A millisecond is
questions.a: A millisecond is one-thousandth of a second. A microsecond is one-millionth of a second.
o: one-thousandth of a second
one-millionth of a second
one-hundredth of a second
one-thousandth of a minute

questions.q: At the district meet two sprinters seem to cross the line together. The school wall clock shows time only to the nearest second. Which would best decide the winner?
questions.a: Close finishes need fractions of a second, which the chapter says sports timing devices record. The wall clock's smallest interval is 1 s.
o: An electronic timer reading hundredths or thousandths of a second
The school wall clock whose smallest division is one second
A sundial placed beside the finish line to read the shadow
An hourglass that empties in exactly one minute of sand

questions.q: Which statement about units of time is false?
questions.a: Symbols are written in singular, so 5 mins is wrong; it should be 5 min.
o: Symbols take a plural form, for example 5 mins
The SI unit of time is the second, whose symbol is s
60 minutes make 1 hour, so 60 min = 1 h
Symbols such as s, min and h are written in lowercase

questions.q: Meera says a pendulum clock and an atomic clock are completely different in principle. Her teacher says there is one idea common to both. What is it?
questions.a: All clocks, old or modern, rely on a process that repeats continuously and marks equal intervals of time.
o: Both rely on a process that repeats to mark equal intervals
Both use the changing shadow of an object lit by the Sun
Both use sand flowing steadily from one bulb to another
Both use water flowing steadily into a vessel with marks

questions.q: Which of the following is written correctly according to the rules of the chapter?
questions.a: The symbol of second is s, written lowercase after a space. 'sec', 'secs' and '45s' break the rules.
o: The race took 45 s
The race took 45 sec
The race took 45s
The race took 45 secs

questions.q: (a) Convert 2.5 h into minutes. (b) Convert the result into seconds.
s: Part (a): 2.5 x 60 = 150 min

questions.q: A student says, "A pendulum clock and an atomic clock are equally good, since both are based on something repeating." Test this with the chapter's facts: (i) the common principle, (ii) how far Huygens' early clock could drift in 30 days at 10 s a day, (iii) the atomic clock's error, (iv) your verdict on the statement, (v) which you would use to time a close sprint and why.
questions.a: Both rely on a repeating process, but Huygens' early clock could drift 30 x 10 = 300 s = 5 min in 30 days, while an atomic clock loses one second in millions of years. Same principle, different precision. A sprint needs precise electronic timing.
s: Common principle: a continuously repeating process marks equal intervals
30 x 10 = 300 s = 5 minutes of drift
Atomic clocks lose only one second in millions of years
Verdict: same principle but very different precision, so the statement is wrong
Sprint timing: a precise electronic timer, since close races need fractions of a second

questions.q: A song lasts 3 min 20 s. (a) Express its length in seconds. (b) How many such songs can be played back to back in 1 hour?
questions.a: (a) 200 s. (b) 18 songs.
s: Part (b): 3600 / 200 = 18 songs

questions.q:
At the state athletics meet the girls' 100 m final is timed electronically to one-thousandth of a second: the winner took 12.482 s and the runner-up 12.487 s. The school wants one timer for its house races, where past gaps between the first two runners were as small as 0.03 s. The options are Timer A showing whole seconds (₹400), Timer B showing hundredths of a second (₹1,500) and Timer C showing thousandths of a second (₹6,000).
(a) Find the gap at the state meet in milliseconds.
(b) Express the school's smallest past gap, 0.03 s, in milliseconds.
(c) How many hundredths of a second is that gap, and which timers can separate the two runners?
(d) Which timer should the school buy, and why?
questions.a: (a) 5 milliseconds. (b) 30 milliseconds. (c) 3 hundredths of a second; B and C can separate them, A cannot. (d) Timer B: hundredths are enough for a 0.03 s gap and it costs ₹4,500 less than C.
s: Part (a): 12.487 - 12.482 = 0.005 s = 5 milliseconds
Part (b): 0.03 x 1000 = 30 milliseconds
Part (c): 3 hundredths; Timers B and C can separate them, Timer A cannot
Part (d): Timer B; it separates a 0.03 s gap at a lower cost than Timer C

questions.q: Sameer says, "A quartz clock and an atomic clock both work by tiny, very rapid vibrations." Check his claim.
questions.a: Right. A quartz clock uses a quartz crystal and an atomic clock uses specific atoms; in both the vibrations repeat and mark equal intervals.
s: Verdict: he is right
Quartz clocks use the vibrations of a quartz crystal
Atomic clocks use vibrations of specific atoms; both repeat and mark equal intervals

questions.q:
A hospital corridor has an old pendulum clock that shows only whole seconds and gains 10 s each day, like Huygens' early clocks. The ECG machine has a quartz-based timer. For one patient the ECG records two heartbeat gaps of 0.75 s and 0.80 s. The drug chart needs times right to the nearest minute, while the ECG analysis needs milliseconds. The hospital can buy one new timer only.
(a) Express 0.75 s in milliseconds.
(b) By how much will the corridor clock be fast after 6 days?
(c) By how many milliseconds do the two heartbeat gaps differ?
(d) Should the hospital buy a quartz timer for the ECG and keep resetting the corridor clock daily, or use the corridor clock for both jobs? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) 750 milliseconds. (b) 60 s = 1 min. (c) 50 milliseconds. (d) Buy the quartz timer for the ECG; the corridor clock, reset daily, is accurate enough for minutes but cannot resolve a 50 millisecond difference.
s: Part (a): 0.75 x 1000 = 750 milliseconds
Part (b): 6 x 10 = 60 s = 1 minute
Part (c): 0.80 - 0.75 = 0.05 s = 50 milliseconds
Part (d): buy the quartz timer for the ECG; a 10 s daily drift is tiny for a drug chart in minutes if reset daily, but whole seconds cannot show a 50 millisecond difference

questions.q: Name two situations from the chapter where very small fractions of a second must be measured.
questions.a: Sports timing to decide winners of a close race; ECG machines measuring millisecond variations in heartbeats (also digital recording and computers).
s: Sports timing to decide winners
ECG machines, digital music recording or computers

questions.q: State two rules for writing units of time and their symbols.
questions.a: Symbols are lowercase and singular without a full stop; a space is left between the number and the unit.
s: Symbols s, min, h in lowercase and singular, no full stop
Leave a space between the number and the unit

questions.q: Which clock is so precise that it loses only one second in millions of years?
questions.a: Atomic clocks use specific atoms and lose only one second in millions of years; Huygens' early pendulum clocks could gain or lose 10 s a day.
o: An atomic clock
Huygens' early pendulum clock
A sinking-bowl water clock
A sundial

questions.q: A notice reads: '8 Sec. for Race 1; Break: 2 hrs; Class: 45mins; Warm-up: 30 Seconds; Total: 3 H'. Rewrite each of the five entries correctly and name the rule broken.
questions.a: 8 s; 2 h; 45 min; 30 s (or 30 seconds, lowercase); 3 h (lowercase).
s: 8 s: symbol is s, with no full stop
2 h: not 'hrs'
45 min: space and singular
30 s or 30 seconds: unit name in lowercase
3 h: symbol h is lowercase

questions.q:
Statement I: The SI unit of time is the second, with symbol s.
Statement II: 'sec' and 'hrs' are correct symbols for second and hour.
Statement III: Quartz clocks work by vibrations of specific atoms.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Only I is correct. II is false: 'sec' and 'hrs' are incorrect. III is false: quartz clocks use a quartz crystal; atomic clocks use atoms.
o: I only
I and II only
I and III only
II and III only

questions.q: An ECG shows one heartbeat gap of 0.8 s. (a) Express it in milliseconds. (b) How many such beats occur in 1 minute? (c) Write the gap in seconds and the time for the beats with correct unit symbols.
questions.a: (a) 800 milliseconds. (b) 75 beats in 1 minute. (c) 0.8 s and 75 beats in 1 min.
s: Part (a): 0.8 x 1000 = 800 milliseconds
Part (b): 60 / 0.8 = 75 beats
Part (c): writes 0.8 s and 1 min with lowercase singular symbols and a space

questions.q: Two runners finish at 12.35 s and 12.55 s. Show that a wall clock whose smallest division is 1 s cannot tell which one won.
questions.a: Both times lie within the same 1 s division (12 to 13 s), so the clock shows no difference. A timer of fractions of a second is needed.
s: The smallest interval of the clock is 1 s
Both times lie between 12 s and 13 s, so the clock shows the same reading
A device recording tenths or hundredths of a second is needed

questions.q: Rewrite correctly: '30 Secs.' and '2 Hrs' (inside a sentence).
questions.a: 30 s and 2 h: lowercase symbols, singular, no full stop, with a space after the number.
s: 2 h

questions.q: A train covers the 200 km between two stations in 2.5 hours. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: Speed = 200 / 2.5 = 80 km/h, an average. Multiplying gives 500, a wrong operation; inverting gives h/km, which is not speed.
o: Its average speed is 80 km/h, though it may have varied
It moved at exactly 80 km/h at every single instant of the journey
Its speed is 500 km/h, found by multiplying the distance and the time
Its speed is 0.0125 h/km, found by dividing the time by the distance

questions.q: Runners A and B start together. Runner A completes 400 m in 50 s and runner B completes 300 m in 40 s. (a) Find the speed of each. (b) Who is faster and by how much? (c) How far does A run in 2 minutes at this speed? (d) How far does B run in the same time? (e) State how much A is ahead then.
questions.a: A = 8 m/s, B = 7.5 m/s; A is faster by 0.5 m/s. In 120 s A runs 960 m and B 900 m, so A leads by 60 m.
s: Part (a): A = 8 m/s, B = 7.5 m/s
Part (b): A is faster by 0.5 m/s
Part (e): A leads by 60 m

questions.q: Tanvi walks 900 m to the market in 10 minutes. Which working gives her speed in m/s?
questions.a: Convert 10 min to 600 s first: 900 / 600 = 1.5 m/s. 90 'm/s' forgets to convert minutes to seconds.
o: 900 m divided by 600 s = 1.5 m/s
900 m divided by 10 min = 90 m/s
600 s divided by 900 m = 0.67 s/m

questions.q: A cyclist covers 21.6 km in 1.5 h. (a) Find her speed in km/h. (b) Express it in m/s.
Which is faster, 54 km/h or 12 m/s? Convert 54 km/h into m/s, convert 12 m/s into km/h, and then justify your decision.
questions.a: 54 km/h = 15 m/s and 12 m/s = 43.2 km/h. Since 15 > 12 (or 54 > 43.2), 54 km/h is faster.
s: 54 km/h: 54 x 1000 / 3600 method shown
54 km/h = 15 m/s
12 m/s: 12 x 3600 / 1000 method shown
Concludes 54 km/h is faster, in either unit

questions.q: Cyclist A covers 900 m in 3 minutes and cyclist B covers 1000 m in 4 minutes. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: Speed = distance / time: A = 300 m/min, B = 250 m/min. Comparing distance alone ignores time.
o: A is faster, covering 300 m a minute against 250 m a minute
B is faster, because B covered the greater distance of 1000 m
They are equally fast, since both rode for only a few minutes
B is faster, because B rode for the longer time of 4 minutes

questions.q:
On Sports Day three teams each ran a different race length on a straight track. Team Red ran 400 m in 80 s, Team Blue ran 300 m in 50 s and Team Green ran 200 m in 36 s. The teacher must choose one team to represent the school at the district event, and a student argues that Red should go because it ran the farthest.
(a) Find the speed of Red.
(b) Which is faster, Blue or Green, and by how much, correct to two decimal places?
(c) How long would Blue take to run 400 m at its speed?
(d) Which team should the teacher choose, and is the student's argument sound?
questions.a: (a) 5 m/s. (b) Blue (6 m/s) is faster than Green (5.56 m/s) by 0.44 m/s. (c) 66.7 s. (d) Blue; Red ran farthest but has the lowest speed.
s: Part (b): Blue 6 m/s, Green 5.56 m/s; Blue faster by 0.44 m/s
Part (d): Blue, with the highest speed; the argument is unsound since distance alone does not decide speed

questions.q:
Statement I: Speed is the total distance covered divided by the total time taken.
Statement II: A bus moving at 50 km/h for 2 h covers 100 km.
Statement III: The time taken to cover a distance is the distance divided by the speed.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: All three are correct: speed = distance / time; 50 x 2 = 100 km; time = distance / speed.
o: I, II and III
I and II only
II and III only
I and III only

questions.q: Rohit says, "A car that has travelled 120 km must have a higher speed than a scooter that has travelled 40 km." Check this claim with an example.
questions.a: Not necessarily. If the car takes 3 h its speed is 40 km/h; if the scooter takes 0.5 h its speed is 80 km/h.
s: Verdict: not necessarily true
Speed depends on distance per unit time, so time must be known
Example: car 120 km in 3 h = 40 km/h; scooter 40 km in 0.5 h = 80 km/h

questions.q: Priya says she cycled 15 km in 30 minutes, so her speed was 50 km/h. Show that this cannot be right.
questions.a: 15 km / 0.5 h = 30 km/h. At 50 km/h she would cover 25 km in 30 min, not 15.
s: 30 minutes = 0.5 h
Speed = 15 / 0.5 = 30 km/h
30 km/h is not 50 km/h; at 50 km/h she would cover 25 km in 30 min

questions.q: Define speed and state its SI unit.
questions.a: Speed is the total distance covered divided by the total time taken; SI unit metre per second (m/s).
s: Total distance covered divided by total time taken
m/s

questions.q: Make up a short real-life situation, with a distance and a time, in which the speed works out to 60 km/h. Show the working.
questions.a: Example: a bus covers 180 km from Pune to a town in 3 h. 180 / 3 = 60 km/h.
s: Situation with a distance and a time
Divides distance by time
Gets 60 km/h with correct units

questions.q: A bus moves at 45 km/h. (a) How far does it go in 2.4 h? (b) How long will it take to cover 63 km, in minutes?
questions.a: (a) 108 km. (b) 1.4 h = 84 minutes.
s: Part (a): 45 x 2.4 = 108 km

questions.q: A bus keeps a speed of 40 km/h for 3 hours. How far does it go?
questions.a: Distance = speed x time = 40 x 3 = 120 km. 13.3 km divides 40 by 3; 43 km adds; 0.075 km is 3 / 40.
o: 120 km
43 km

questions.q:
Between Station P and Station Q, 108 km apart, three trains run. The passenger train takes 3 h, the express takes 1.5 h and the superfast takes 1.2 h. Fares are ₹60, ₹120 and ₹180 respectively. Mr Rao leaves Station P at 8:00 am and must reach Station Q by 9:45 am. He wants the cheapest train that gets him there in time.
(a) Find the speed of each train in km/h.
(b) Express the express train's speed in m/s.
(c) At the superfast's speed, how long would it need for 270 km?
(d) Which train should Mr Rao take? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) 36, 72, 90 km/h. (b) 20 m/s. (c) 3 h. (d) Express: arrives 9:30 am for ₹120; superfast also in time but costs ₹180; passenger is late.
s: Part (a): 36, 72 and 90 km/h
Part (d): express; it arrives at 9:30 am and is cheaper than the superfast; the passenger train arrives at 11:00 am

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The SI unit of speed is metre per second (m/s).
Reason (R): Speed is distance divided by time, and the SI units of length and time are the metre and the second.
questions.a: Both true and R explains A: speed is length per time, so with the SI units of length and time it is metre per second.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
Match Column I with Column II.
1. Speed of an object
2. Distance covered
3. Time taken
4. SI unit of speed
a. metre per second (m/s)
b. Total distance covered divided by total time taken
c. Speed multiplied by time
d. Distance divided by speed
questions.a: Speed = distance / time (b); distance = speed x time (c); time = distance / speed (d); SI unit m/s (a).

questions.q: Meena solved: "A train covers 270 km in 4.5 h. Speed = time / distance = 4.5 / 270 = 0.0167." Find her error and give the correct speed.
questions.a: She inverted the formula. Speed = distance / time = 270 / 4.5 = 60 km/h.
s: Error: she divided time by distance instead of distance by time
Correct speed = 270 / 4.5 = 60 km/h

questions.q: A car moves at 72 km/h. What is its speed in m/s?
questions.a: 72 x 1000 / 3600 = 20 m/s (multiply by 5/18). 259.2 comes from multiplying by 18/5, the flipped rule.
o: 20 m/s

questions.q: Which statement about speed is false?
questions.a: The false statement ignores time; distance must be compared for the same time, or speed must be calculated.
o: A runner who covers more distance is always the faster runner
If two runners run for equal time, the one covering more distance is faster
The SI unit of speed is metre per second
In this book the word speed means average speed

questions.q: Why can we not compare a 100 m runner and a 400 m runner by their finishing times alone? What should we calculate?
questions.a: Different distances make the times unfair to compare; we find each runner's speed.
s: The distances are different, so times alone are not comparable
Calculate speed, distance divided by time, for each

questions.q: At the start of a journey the odometer of a car reads 12,340 km and at the end it reads 12,400 km. The journey took 1.5 h. What is the average speed?
questions.a: Distance = 12,400 - 12,340 = 60 km; speed = 60 / 1.5 = 40 km/h. 60 km/h forgets to divide by time; 90 multiplies.
o: 40 km/h
60 km/h
90 km/h

questions.q: Which statement about uniform and non-uniform motion is false?
questions.a: The chapter says we seldom find uniform motion over long distances in everyday life; that is why average speeds are used.
o: Uniform motion over long distances is always found in everyday life
Uniform linear motion is an idealisation
In non-uniform motion unequal distances are covered in equal intervals
A bus covering 6 km in every 10 minutes on a straight road is in uniform motion

questions.q: Train M covers 30 km in each of the four 15-minute intervals between 10:00 and 11:00. Train N covers 20, 40, 25 and 35 km in the same four intervals. Sunita says, "Both are in uniform motion, since both cover 120 km in the hour." Check her claim.
questions.a: Wrong. Equal averages (120 km/h) do not make motion uniform; N covers 20, 40, 25 and 35 km in equal intervals, so it is non-uniform, while M is uniform.
s: Verdict: wrong
Both cover 120 km in 1 h, so both have an average speed of 120 km/h
N covers unequal distances in equal intervals, so only M is uniform

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of uniform linear motion?
questions.a: Uniform linear motion means equal distances in equal intervals along a straight line.
o: A scooter on a straight road covering 15 m every second
A bus covering 10 m, 14 m and 18 m in successive seconds
A cyclist slowing down at a traffic signal
A train starting from a station

questions.q: On a straight highway a car covers 10 km in the first 10 minutes, 5 km in the next 10 minutes and 10 km in the next 10 minutes. What type of motion is this?
questions.a: Equal intervals but unequal distances (10, 5, 10 km) means non-uniform motion. An average speed exists for any motion.
o: Non-uniform, as unequal distances are covered in equal times
Uniform, since the car keeps moving in one direction only
Uniform, since all three time intervals are of equal length
Uniform, since an average speed can be worked out for it

questions.q:
Neha's father starts a car journey at 8:00 am when the odometer reads 24,560 km. At 10:30 am it reads 24,710 km. During the drive Neha notes the speedometer reading 60 km/h on the highway, 20 km/h in a town and 0 at a railway gate. They have 90 km more to go and must reach her grandmother's house by 1:00 pm.
(a) How far has the car gone by 10:30 am?
(b) Find the average speed so far.
(c) Is the motion uniform? Justify using the speedometer readings.
(d) If the car keeps this average speed, will they arrive before 1:00 pm? Decide.
questions.a: (a) 150 km. (b) 60 km/h. (c) Non-uniform. (d) 1.5 h more, so 12:00 noon, which is before 1:00 pm.
s: Part (c): non-uniform, since the speedometer shows different speeds including 0
Part (d): 90 / 60 = 1.5 h, so arrival at 12:00 noon, before 1:00 pm

questions.q:
During a cross-country run on a straight road, the coach records Varun's distance in each 2-minute interval: 500 m, 500 m, 500 m, 600 m and 400 m. She says, "His average speed is 15 km/h, so he ran steadily throughout."
(a) For which intervals was his motion uniform, and at what speed in m/min?
(b) Find his total distance and average speed in km/h.
(c) Is the whole run uniform? Give the evidence.
(d) Evaluate the coach's statement.
questions.a: (a) First three intervals, 250 m/min. (b) 2500 m, 15 km/h. (c) No, distances 600 m and 400 m are unequal. (d) Average speed 15 km/h is correct, but the run was not steady.
s: Part (a): first three intervals, 500 / 2 = 250 m/min
Part (b): 2500 m in 10 min = 2.5 km in 1/6 h = 15 km/h
Part (c): no; 600 m and 400 m differ from 500 m in equal intervals
Part (d): the average is right but 'steadily' is wrong, since the speed changed

questions.q: The instrument fitted in a vehicle that records the distance travelled in kilometres is the
questions.a: The odometer measures distance in km; the speedometer shows speed in km/h.
o: odometer
speedometer
stopwatch
hourglass

questions.q: An object in uniform motion covers 12 m in 4 s. How far does it go in 10 s?
questions.a: Speed = 12 / 4 = 3 m/s; distance = 3 x 10 = 30 m. 48 m is 12 x 4; 120 m is 12 x 10; 22 m adds.

questions.q: Differentiate between a speedometer and an odometer.
questions.a: A speedometer displays speed in km/h; an odometer records the distance travelled in km.
s: Speedometer shows the speed of the vehicle in km/h
Odometer records the distance travelled in km

questions.q: A car covers 45 km, 55 km and 35 km in three successive hours. (a) Find its average speed. (b) Is its motion uniform? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) 135 km / 3 h = 45 km/h. (b) Not uniform, since the distances 45, 55, 35 km in equal hours are unequal.
s: Part (a): 135 / 3 = 45 km/h
Part (b): not uniform; unequal distances in equal hours

questions.q: An object is at 0 m at 0 s, 20 m at 10 s, 38 m at 20 s and 60 m at 30 s. Show that its motion cannot be uniform.
questions.a: The distances are 20, 18 and 22 m in successive 10 s, so unequal; therefore the motion is not uniform.
s: Finds distances in each interval: 20 m, 18 m, 22 m
These are unequal in equal 10 s intervals
Uniform motion needs equal distances in equal intervals

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A bus that covers 6 km in every 10 minutes along a straight road for an hour is in uniform linear motion.
Reason (R): The bus covers a total of 36 km in that hour.
questions.a: Both true, but R does not explain A; the reason is that the bus covers equal distances (6 km) in equal intervals.
o: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q: What is average speed? Why does the book use the word speed for it?
questions.a: It is total distance divided by total time. Objects seldom keep constant speed, so the book uses speed to mean average speed.
s: Total distance covered divided by total time taken
The speed of an object usually changes, so the calculated value is an average

questions.q:
Statement I: In uniform linear motion the speed of the object keeps changing.
Statement II: Speed found as total distance divided by total time is the average speed.
Statement III: An odometer records the distance travelled by a vehicle in kilometres.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: II and III are correct. I is false: in uniform linear motion the speed is constant.
o: II and III only
I and II only
I and III only
I, II and III

questions.q: A vehicle moves along a straight line. It covers the first 1000 m at 10 m/s and the next 1000 m at 5 m/s. At what speed must it cover a further 1000 m so that the whole journey of 3000 m takes 400 s? Also find the average speed. (a) time for the first part, (b) for the second, (c) time left, (d) required speed, (e) average speed.
What is linear motion? Give one example from the chapter.
questions.a: Motion of an object along a straight line, for example a train between two adjacent stations.
s: Motion along a straight line
Example such as a train between two adjacent stations

questions.q: Car P covers 15 m in every 5 s for 25 s. Car Q covers 10 m, 20 m, 15 m, 20 m and 10 m in successive 5 s intervals. Compare their motion: (a) type of P, (b) type of Q, (c) average speeds, (d) what the equal averages show, (e) which type is more common in daily life.
questions.a: P is uniform; Q is non-uniform. Both cover 75 m in 25 s, an average of 3 m/s, so equal averages can hide different motion. Non-uniform motion is more common in everyday life.
s: Part (a): P is uniform, equal distances in equal intervals
Part (b): Q is non-uniform, unequal distances
Part (c): both 75 m in 25 s = 3 m/s
Part (d): equal average speed does not mean same type of motion
Part (e): non-uniform is more common; uniform motion is an idealisation

questions.q: Make up a short story of a scooter journey in which the motion is uniform for one part and non-uniform for another part.
questions.a: Example: A scooter leaves a lane slowly and speeds up (non-uniform), then runs at 40 km/h for 10 minutes on a straight highway (uniform), then slows at a toll booth (non-uniform).
s: Uniform part described with constant speed
Non-uniform part described with speeding up or slowing down
Labels each part correctly with a reason

questions.q: A car covers 5, 8, 7, 10, 6 and 4 km in six successive 10-minute intervals. (a) Find its average speed in km/h. (b) In which interval did it cover the most distance?
questions.a: (a) 5+8+7+10+6+4 = 40 km in 60 min = 40 km/h. (b) The fourth interval, 10 km.
s: Part (a): 40 km in 1 h = 40 km/h
Part (b): the fourth interval, 10 km
